title: Quillen B base change along a discrete fibration
statement:
Use small ordinary categories, nerves and weak homotopy types as in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Let $U:\mathcal E\to\mathcal B$ be a functor. For $b\in\mathcal B$, the comma category $(U\downarrow b)$ has objects $(e,\alpha:Ue\to b)$ and arrows $h:e\to e'$ with $\alpha' U(h)=\alpha$. Suppose that for every arrow $\beta:b_0\to b_1$, postcomposition induces a weak homotopy equivalence $N(U\downarrow b_0)\to N(U\downarrow b_1)$. Let $V:\mathcal D\to\mathcal B$ be a discrete fibration: for every $d\in\mathcal D$ and arrow $b\to Vd$ there is a unique arrow $d'\to d$ over it. Form the strict pullback category $\mathcal E\times_{\mathcal B}\mathcal D$. Then the square of nerves
$$\begin{matrix}N(\mathcal E\times_{\mathcal B}\mathcal D)&\longrightarrow&N\mathcal E\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow NU\\ N\mathcal D&\xrightarrow{NV}&N\mathcal B\end{matrix}$$
is a homotopy-pullback square of weak homotopy types. A homotopy pullback of weak homotopy types is computed after Kan replacements of the cospan by the path-space model $A\times_{C,\operatorname{ev}_0}\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,C)\times_{\operatorname{ev}_1,C}B$; a square is a homotopy-pullback square when its coherence-induced comparison to this model is a weak homotopy equivalence. The comparison is the one induced by this strict square and is natural for commutative maps of such diagrams. No fibrant-category axioms, localization or model structure on any of the ordinary categories is assumed.

source.place: Dual of Proposition 4.6.11, using the overcategory form of the local-constancy test in Lemma 4.6.9; applied to nerves of ordinary categories, since the nerve of a discrete fibration is a right fibration. Compare Corollary 4.6.12. Online PDF read on 2026-10-17; local archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this result.

proof.text: Put $\mathcal P=\mathcal E\times_{\mathcal B}\mathcal D$, with projections $a:\mathcal P\to\mathcal E$ and $\pi:\mathcal P\to\mathcal D$. An object is $(e,d')$ with $Ue=Vd'$; an arrow is $(h,k)$ with $Uh=Vk$. The equality $Ua=V\pi$ holds on objects and arrows. In each degree a functor $[n]\to\mathcal P$ is exactly a pair of functors to $\mathcal E,\mathcal D$ agreeing in $\mathcal B$, so this is the indicated strict square of nerves.

source.place: Corollary 4.6.12, printed p. 183 (PDF p. 198), applied to opposite categories; its overcategory form, followed by contraction of B/b to its terminal object, gives the comma homotopy-fiber comparison. Read online on 2026-10-17; archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this theorem.

proof.text: For $d\in\mathcal D$, define $\Phi_d:(\pi\downarrow d)\to(U\downarrow Vd)$ by $((e,d'),\delta:d'\to d)\mapsto(e,V\delta)$, and $(h,k)\mapsto h$. For $(e,\alpha:Ue\to Vd)$ the unique lift of $\alpha$ with target $d$ supplies $\delta:d'\to d$ with $Vd'=Ue$, hence an inverse on objects. For $h:(e,\alpha)\to(e',\alpha')$, let $\delta':d''\to d$ be the lift of $\alpha'$ and lift $Uh:Ue\to Ue'$ with target $d''$ to $k:\widetilde d\to d''$. The composite $\delta'k$ and $\delta$ lift the same arrow $\alpha$ with target $d$, so uniqueness gives $\widetilde d=d'$ and $\delta'k=\delta$. Thus $(h,k)$ is the required comma arrow. Unique lifting of identities and composites verifies the functor laws and both inverse identities. Consequently $\Phi_d$ is an isomorphism, not just a weak equivalence. For $\epsilon:d_0\to d_1$, postcomposition by $\epsilon$ corresponds under these isomorphisms to postcomposition by $V\epsilon$. Therefore all comma-transition nerves for $\pi$ are weak equivalences by the hypothesis on $U$. These constructions also commute with strictly commuting maps of the original diagrams, since such functors send a lift to the unique lift with its specified target.

source.place: Corollary 4.6.12, printed p. 183 (PDF p. 198), applied to opposite categories; its overcategory form, followed by contraction of B/b to its terminal object, gives the comma homotopy-fiber comparison. Read online on 2026-10-17; archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this theorem.

proof.text: Use the functorial Kan replacement $R(K)=\operatorname{Sing}(|K|)$. It is Kan: under realization--singular adjunction a horn map into $R(K)$ is a map $|\Lambda_i^n|\to|K|$, and the horn-pair homeomorphism in [lem-coef-realization-finite-limits] supplies a retraction $|\Delta^n|\to|\Lambda_i^n|$. The characteristic-map unit is a weak equivalence for every $K$ by [lem-cbc-realization-singular-unit-weak]. Choose once a universe containing all the sets of continuous maps used here; the four categories and their commas are small in it. Set $X=RN\mathcal P$, $A=RN\mathcal E$, $Z=RN\mathcal D$, $C=RN\mathcal B$, $r=RN\pi$, $f=RNU$, $v=RNV$, $u=RNa$. These are Kan complexes and $fu=vr$ strictly.

source.place: Theorem 3.6.4.1 for the unit; realized horn-pair retraction and the adjunction are the existing realization-finite-limits statement.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-quillen-b-comma-homotopy-fiber] to $U$ and to $\pi$, whose hypothesis was verified in Step 2. For every original category object $d$, its naturality for the square $(a,V)$ identifies the induced map $\operatorname{hofib}_{d}(r)\to\operatorname{hofib}_{Vd}(f)$ with $RN\Phi_d$ through the two comma comparisons. Both comparisons are weak equivalences and $RN\Phi_d$ is an isomorphism, so this particular homotopy-fiber map is a weak equivalence: on components and on every homotopy group its map is the composite of isomorphisms. This proves more than an abstract equivalence of fibers; it identifies the map induced by the strict square.

source.place: Corollary 4.6.12, printed p. 183 (PDF p. 198), applied to opposite categories; its overcategory form, followed by contraction of B/b to its terminal object, gives the comma homotopy-fiber comparison. Read online on 2026-10-17; archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this theorem.

proof.text: Form $Q=A\times_{C,\operatorname{ev}_0}\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,C)\times_{\operatorname{ev}_1,C}Z$, and let $q:Q\to Z$ be the last projection. By [lem-coef-space-path-fibration-replacement] the mapping-path projection for $f$ is a Kan fibration; its pullback $q$ is Kan because a horn lifting square in a pullback is exactly a horn lifting square upstairs with the base coordinate retained. Since $Z$ is Kan, projected-horn filling followed by this lifting shows $Q$ Kan. Define $k:X\to Q$ by $x\mapsto(u(x),\operatorname{const}_{fu(x)},r(x))$. The equality $fu=vr$ makes this well-defined. For any vertex $z$ of $Z$, the strict fiber $Q_z$ is exactly $\operatorname{hofib}_{v(z)}(f)$. Apply [lem-cbc-right-fibration-space-fiber] to $q$ (a Kan fibration lifts every positive-index horn): its natural constant-path map $j_z:Q_z\to\operatorname{hofib}_z(q)$ is a weak equivalence. Define $F_z=\operatorname{hofib}_z(r)$ and $g_z:F_z\to Q_z$ by $(x,\gamma)\mapsto(u(x),v\gamma,z)$. For an original object $z=d$, this is exactly the strict-square homotopy-fiber map of Step 4, so $g_d$ is a weak equivalence. Write $h_z:F_z\to\operatorname{hofib}_z(q)$ for the fiber map of $k$, namely $(x,\gamma)\mapsto(k(x),\gamma)$. There is a specific simplicial homotopy from $h_z$ to $j_zg_z$: at interval parameter $t$ send $(x,\gamma)$ to the $Q$-point $(u(x),s\mapsto v\gamma(\min(s,t)),\gamma(t))$, together with the final $Z$-path $s\mapsto\gamma(\max(s,t))$. The order-preserving functions $\min,\max:[1]\times[1]\to[1]$ induce simplicial maps. Thus these formulas apply to $n$-simplices with their $\Delta^n$ parameter retained and commute with every simplicial operator. The first path starts at $v r(x)=f u(x)$ and ends at $v\gamma(t)$; the second starts at $\gamma(t)$ and ends at $z$. At $t=0$ the first path is constant and the second is $\gamma$, giving $h_z$; at $t=1$ they are $v\gamma$ and the constant path at $z$, giving $j_zg_z$. To justify weak-equivalence invariance under this homotopy without a basepoint assumption, the projection $p:F_z\times\Delta^1\to F_z$ is a simplicial homotopy equivalence: its section at $0$ is an inverse, with cylinder contraction $(x,t,s)\mapsto(x,\min(t,s))$. By [lem-cbc-simplicial-homotopy-equivalence-weak], $p$ is a weak equivalence; since $p i_0=p i_1=1$, both endpoint inclusions are weak equivalences on components and all groups. If $z=d$, the homotopy $H$ has $H i_1=j_dg_d$ a weak equivalence, so $H$ and then $H i_0=h_d$ are weak equivalences by composing these isomorphisms. Therefore the particular fiber map $\operatorname{hofib}_d(k)$ is a weak equivalence for every original object $d$.

source.place: Path-space fibration replacement and fiber comparison as in the cited existing nodes; explicit min/max interval homotopy identifies the particular fiber map. Simplicial homotopy-equivalence input: Kerodon 00UB, via its cited node.

proof.text: Here original objects suffice, despite the extra vertices of $Z=\operatorname{Sing}|N\mathcal D|$. Replace $r:X\to Z$ and $q:Q\to Z$ by their mapping-path fibrations, using [lem-coef-space-path-fibration-replacement]. The map $k$ induces a map of these fibrations over $Z$, sending $(x,\gamma)$ to $(k(x),\gamma)$; its strict vertex-fiber maps are exactly $\operatorname{hofib}_z(k)$. For any vertex $z$ of $Z$, regard it as a point of $|N\mathcal D|$ and choose a simplex representing it. The straight segment in that topological simplex to any of its vertices is a singular edge in $Z$ joining $z$ to the image of an original object $d$. Pull the two mapping-path fibrations back along this edge $\Delta^1\to Z$. They remain Kan fibrations by the explicit lifting argument of Step 5; their realizations are Serre fibrations by [lem-coef-kan-realization-serre], and realization identifies their endpoint fibers with the realized simplicial fibers by [lem-coef-realization-finite-limits]. For a Serre fibration over $|\Delta^1|=[0,1]$, inclusion of either endpoint fiber in the total space is a weak equivalence: in the exact sequence of [lem-coef-serre-homotopy-exact-sequence] all positive homotopy groups of the base vanish, while path lifting and the orbit/stabilizer clause with trivial $\pi_1([0,1])$ identify components. This holds at every fiber basepoint; every total-space component meets each endpoint fiber by path lifting. The interval is contracted by $(t,s)\mapsto(1-s)t$ (or $1-(1-s)(1-t)$ at the other endpoint), so the asserted vanishing is explicit. Naturality of that exact sequence gives a commutative square of the endpoint-fiber inclusion maps for our map of fibrations. The weak equivalence at endpoint $d$ from Step 5 therefore implies weak equivalence of the map of total spaces, and then weak equivalence at endpoint $z$, by composing the component and group isomorphisms. If one endpoint fiber is empty, path lifting makes the total space and other endpoint fiber empty as well. We have proved $\operatorname{hofib}_z(k)$ weakly equivalent for every vertex $z$ of $Z$.

source.place: Corollary 3.6.2 (realized Kan fibrations); Lemma 2.4.16 and Proposition 2.4.18 (natural exact sequence and component/path-lifting argument). Applied only through the cited DAG statements.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-spaces-homotopy-fiber-detection] to $k:X\to Q$ over $\mathrm{id}_Z$, with the constant homotopy witnessing $qk=r$. All four spaces $X,Q,Z,Z$ are Kan (Steps 3 and 5), the base map is an identity weak equivalence, and all vertex-fiber maps are weak equivalences by Step 6. It follows that $k$ is a weak equivalence. By the displayed path-space definition in the statement, this says exactly that the original square is a homotopy pullback of weak homotopy types, using the functorial Kan replacement of Step 3. The map $k$ is the constant-path comparison induced by the given strict square, not a chosen abstract equivalence. For commutative maps of such diagrams the nerve, $R$, pullback coordinates, and constant-path maps commute; consequently these comparisons are natural, with the higher simplices retained degree by degree. All auxiliary choices in Step 6 certify weak equivalence only and do not enter $k$. If $\mathcal D$ is empty, both $X$ and $Q$ are empty and the same conclusion is immediate; if $\mathcal B$ is empty all the categories mapping to it are empty. No model structure on ordinary categories was used.
